source_text: Die quo in neruo mansimus ostensum est mihi hoc. Uideo locum illum quem retro uideram, et Dinocraten mundo corpore, bene uestitum, refrigerantem; et ubi erat uulnus, uideo cicatricem: et piscina illa summisso margine usque ad umbilicum pueri; et aquam de ea trahebat sine cessatione. Et super marginem fiala aurea plena aqua; et accessit Dinocrates et de ea bibere coepit; quae fiala non deficiebat. Et satiatus accessit ludere de aqua more infantium gaudens. Et experrecta sum. Et intellexi translatum eum esse de poena.
orientation: Perpetua, writing her prison diary, reports what she saw after praying day and night for her dead young brother Dinocrates.
pass_a_gloss: On the day on which we remained in the stocks this was shown to me. I see that place which I had seen before, and Dinocrates with clean body, well clothed, experiencing relief; and where the wound had been, I see a scar; and that pool with its rim lowered all the way to the navel of the boy; and he was drawing water from it without stopping. And upon the rim a golden bowl full of water; and Dinocrates approached and began to drink from it; which bowl was not running out. And having had enough he went to play with water in the manner of infants rejoicing. And I awoke. And I understood that he had been transferred from punishment.

choices.why: means wooden stocks in prison context, not generic chains
brief glossary fixes relief for refrigerare, covering relief from postmortem suffering
keeps literal bodily contrast with earlier disfigured suffering body

choices.english: he had been transferred from punishment
choices.why: translatum echoes transfer language and de poena is separation from suffering, not full verdict on afterlife
rejected: he had been delivered from torment
he was taken out of suffering

pass_b_english: On the day we spent in the stocks, this was shown to me. I see the same place I had seen before, and Dinocrates is there with a clean body, well clothed, experiencing relief. Where the wound had been, I see a scar. That pool now has its rim lowered to the boy's navel, and he is drawing water from it without stopping. A golden bowl full of water stands on the rim, and Dinocrates steps up and begins to drink from it, and the bowl never runs dry. When he has had his fill, he goes off to play joyfully with the water as children do. Then I woke, and I understood that he had been transferred from punishment.
